name: Keto diet
summary: A keto diet is very low in carbohydrate and high in fat, so the body makes ketones as an extra fuel. Over a year or more it led to a little more weight loss than low-fat diets and lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, but LDL cholesterol often rose. Its best-proven use is as a medical treatment for epilepsy that medicines do not control.
howItWorks: With very little carbohydrate, the liver turns fat into ketones, which the brain and muscles can use as fuel. This state is called ketosis.
Fewer carbohydrates usually means lower blood sugar and insulin after meals. Some of the weight and blood sugar changes in trials may come from this, and some from simply eating fewer calories.
Many people feel tired, dizzy or get headaches in the first days or weeks (called the keto flu). These symptoms are known mainly from forum posts, not from controlled studies.
For epilepsy, how the diet reduces seizures is not fully understood. It is used under a specialist team, mostly in children whose seizures medicines do not control.
whatStudiesDid: In the weight-loss trials, adults on a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet (no more than 50 g of carbohydrate a day) were compared with adults on a conventional low-fat diet for 12 months or more. The type 2 diabetes review pooled 23 trials of low-carbohydrate diets (under 130 g a day, or under 26% of a 2,000 kcal diet) and very low-carbohydrate diets (under 10% of calories) lasting at least 12 weeks. The epilepsy trials tested classic ketogenic diets, medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) versions and the modified Atkins diet, mostly in children, under the care of a specialist team. Studies of long-term outcomes such as deaths followed large groups of people and scored how low in carbohydrate their usual eating was; most of those people were not in ketosis.

findings.outcome: Body weight compared with a low-fat diet
findings.population: Adults, mostly with overweight or obesity, followed for 12 months or more (13 trials), and adults with overweight or obesity in 14 trials of any length
whyThisGrade: The difference after a year or more was small, under 1 kg on average
People cannot be blinded to what they eat, and diets in the trials were not all alike
The reviews pooled trials of different people and diets
In favour: trials were randomised and the direction was the same in several reviews
findings.summary: A 2013 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials compared a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet (no more than 50 g of carbohydrate a day) with a low-fat diet for 12 months or more. People on the ketogenic diet had lost a little more weight: 0.91 kg more (95% confidence interval 0.17 to 1.65 kg, 1,415 people). A 2020 meta-analysis of 14 trials in people with overweight or obesity also found more weight loss on ketogenic diets than on low-fat diets (standardised mean difference -0.46, p = 0.04), whether or not they had diabetes. A 2020 review of very low-calorie ketogenic programmes (12 studies, where the diets also cut calories sharply) found average weight losses of about 10 kg to 15.6 kg during the ketogenic phase, which stayed stable in follow-up of up to two years. Those programmes were not compared with other diets in the same way, and the weight lost came from cutting calories as well as carbohydrate.
findings.bottomLine: After a year or more, people on a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet had lost about 1 kg more than people on low-fat diets in a 13-trial meta-analysis. The gap is small, and the diets differ a lot between trials.
findings.label: Weight
findings.line: A little more weight loss than low-fat diets after a year or more

findings.outcome: Blood sugar and remission in type 2 diabetes
findings.population: Adults with type 2 diabetes (23 trials of low-carbohydrate and very low-carbohydrate diets, lasting at least 12 weeks)
whyThisGrade: The review rated its evidence moderate to low certainty, and only 40.6% of outcomes had a low risk of bias
Benefits seen at 6 months mostly faded by 12 months
The trials covered low-carbohydrate diets in general, not only ketogenic ones
Remission means different things in different trials, and was much smaller without medicines
findings.summary: A 2021 BMJ review pooled 23 trials (1,357 people with type 2 diabetes) of low-carbohydrate and very low-carbohydrate diets. At 6 months, 57% (76 of 133) of people on these diets reached remission (HbA1c below 6.5%, with or without diabetes medicines) compared with 31% (41 of 131) on control diets (risk difference 0.32, 95% confidence interval 0.17 to 0.47). The effect was smaller and not significant when remission was defined as HbA1c below 6.5% without any medicines. Remission fell markedly in studies that included people using insulin. At 12 months the data on remission were sparse, from a small effect to a trivial increase in risk, and the improvements in weight, triglycerides and insulin sensitivity seen at 6 months had faded. A 2020 meta-analysis of ketogenic diets in 14 trials found lower HbA1c than on low-fat diets in people with diabetes (standardised mean difference -0.62, p < 0.001).
findings.bottomLine: In people with type 2 diabetes, low-carbohydrate diets brought more people to remission at 6 months (57% against 31%), but the benefit faded by 12 months and was smaller without medicines. People on insulin did worse, so medicines need a doctor's involvement.
findings.label: Type 2 diabetes
findings.line: More people in remission at 6 months (57% vs 31%), fading by 12 months

findings.population: Adults following very low-carbohydrate or ketogenic diets, with and without overweight (several meta-analyses)
whyThisGrade: Results differ between reviews: some found LDL cholesterol rising, one found no change
The normal-weight analysis rests on only 3 studies
LDL cholesterol is a marker of heart risk, not a measured heart attack
Results may depend on how much weight people lose and what fats they eat
findings.summary: In the 2013 meta-analysis of 13 trials lasting 12 months or more, LDL cholesterol was 0.12 mmol/L higher on a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet than on a low-fat diet (95% confidence interval 0.04 to 0.2, 1,255 people). In a 2023 meta-analysis of 3 trials in normal-weight adults (body mass index below 25), a ketogenic diet raised LDL cholesterol by 1.08 mmol/L (0.37 to 1.79) and apolipoprotein B by 0.35 g/L (0.06 to 0.65), and also raised HDL cholesterol; the authors suggested normal-weight people should consider the risk of high cholesterol. In the 2021 BMJ review of low-carbohydrate diets in type 2 diabetes, blood lipids did not differ significantly at 6 and 12 months, though LDL cholesterol was clinically worse, but not significantly so, at 12 months. A 2020 review of 12 very low-calorie ketogenic studies found no change in LDL cholesterol.
findings.bottomLine: LDL cholesterol tended to be higher on ketogenic diets in several meta-analyses, by a small amount over a year and by much more in a 3-study analysis of normal-weight adults. One review of calorie-cut ketogenic programmes found no change. It varies from person to person.
findings.label: LDL cholesterol
findings.line: Often higher: +0.12 mmol/L in 13 trials, no change in one review

findings.outcome: Triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and blood pressure
findings.population: Adults in trials of 12 months or more, and people with overweight or obesity in very low-calorie ketogenic programmes
whyThisGrade: The changes in blood pressure were small
Some lab markers improved because people lost weight, not only because of the diet
The review of very low-calorie programmes combined studies without a comparison diet
Results for triglycerides were inconsistent in normal-weight adults
findings.summary: In the 2013 meta-analysis of 13 trials, a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet lowered triglycerides by 0.18 mmol/L (95% confidence interval 0.08 to 0.27) and diastolic blood pressure by 1.43 mmHg (0.37 to 2.49) and raised HDL cholesterol by 0.09 mmol/L (0.06 to 0.12) compared with a low-fat diet. Systolic blood pressure was not among the outcomes that differed significantly. In the 2020 review of 12 very low-calorie ketogenic studies, triglycerides fell by about 30 mg/dl and systolic and diastolic blood pressure by about 8 and 7 mmHg. In the 2023 analysis in normal-weight adults, triglycerides did not differ significantly from control diets.
findings.bottomLine: Compared with low-fat diets, ketogenic diets lowered triglycerides a little, raised HDL cholesterol a little and lowered diastolic blood pressure by about 1 mmHg over a year or more. Larger drops came in programmes that also cut calories heavily.
findings.label: Triglycerides and HDL
findings.line: Triglycerides lower and HDL higher by small amounts over a year

findings.outcome: Seizures in drug-resistant epilepsy (a medical treatment, kept apart from the other findings)
findings.population: Children and adults with epilepsy that medicines had not controlled (13 trials, 932 people), treated by a specialist team
whyThisGrade: All 13 trials were open (no blinding) and small
The Cochrane review rated the evidence low to very low certainty
Evidence in adults is much weaker than in children
The diets are used only with medical supervision, so the results do not apply to a self-started diet
findings.summary: A 2020 Cochrane review included 13 trials with 932 people (711 children and 221 adults) with epilepsy not controlled by medicines. In children, ketogenic diets (classic, medium-chain triglyceride and modified Atkins versions) led to more seizure freedom than usual care (risk ratio 3.16, 95% confidence interval 1.20 to 8.35; 4 studies, 385 children; very low-certainty evidence) and more children with at least half as many seizures (risk ratio 5.80, 3.48 to 9.65; low-certainty evidence). The most common side effects in both groups were vomiting, constipation and diarrhoea. In adults, no one became seizure-free, and the effect on seizure reduction is uncertain. The reviewers concluded that ketogenic diets are a valid option for children whose seizures medicines do not control, with more research needed in adults.
findings.bottomLine: For children whose epilepsy medicines do not control, ketogenic diets led to more seizure freedom and fewer seizures than usual care, but the evidence is low to very low certainty. In adults it is much less clear. This is specialist-supervised treatment, not a general diet.
findings.label: Epilepsy (medical use)
findings.line: Fewer seizures in children when medicines fail; specialist care only

findings.outcome: Long-term health: deaths and heart disease
findings.population: Large groups of adults whose usual eating was low in carbohydrate (not necessarily ketogenic), followed for many years
whyThisGrade: Observational: people were not assigned a diet, and food questionnaires are imprecise
These studies measure low-carbohydrate eating in general, not ketosis, so they do not describe a ketogenic diet itself
What the carbohydrate is replaced with (animal or plant foods) seems to matter
No trial has followed people on a ketogenic diet for years
findings.summary: A 2013 meta-analysis of cohort studies found that, among 272,216 people in 4 cohorts, a high low-carbohydrate score went with a higher risk of death from any cause (pooled risk ratio 1.31, 95% confidence interval 1.07 to 1.59). Risks of death from heart and blood vessel disease (1.10, 0.98 to 1.24; 3 cohorts) and of new cases (0.98, 0.78 to 1.24; 4 cohorts) were not significantly different. In a 2023 study of 371,159 people aged 50 to 71 followed for a median of 23.5 years (165,698 deaths), the highest overall and unhealthy low-carbohydrate scores went with higher death rates (hazard ratios 1.12 to 1.18), while a healthy low-carbohydrate score went with slightly lower mortality (0.95, 0.94 to 0.97). These are links, not proof of cause, and they are not about ketogenic diets in particular.
findings.bottomLine: In large observational studies, low-carbohydrate eating patterns that rely on animal foods went with more deaths over decades, while healthier low-carbohydrate patterns did not. These are links about low-carb eating in general; the long-term effect of a ketogenic diet is unknown.
findings.label: Long-term health
findings.line: Low-carb eating linked to more deaths over decades (a link, not keto itself)

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Diabetes treated with insulin or tablets that can cause low blood sugar
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Eating very little carbohydrate can lower blood sugar quickly, and medicine doses may need to change. In the diabetes review, remission fell markedly in studies that included people using insulin. A doctor or diabetes nurse needs to be involved first.
A ketogenic diet changes the balance of protein, fluid, acid and minerals the body has to handle. Ask a kidney doctor before trying it.
There is not enough research on ketogenic diets in pregnancy. Talk to a doctor or midwife first.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: A past or current eating disorder
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Strict food rules can make an eating disorder worse. A doctor or dietitian can help judge whether any restrictive diet is safe.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: High LDL cholesterol, a family history of early heart disease, or existing heart disease
whoShouldBeCareful.note: LDL cholesterol rose in several reviews and varies a lot between people. A doctor can follow your blood tests during a change in diet.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Liver, pancreas or gallbladder conditions, or rare disorders of fat metabolism
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Ketogenic diets for epilepsy are started by specialist teams who check for these first. Ask a doctor before starting a ketogenic diet.
Ketogenic diets are used for epilepsy only under a specialist paediatric team, with regular check-ups. They are not tested as a diet for weight loss in children.

cautions: Headache, tiredness, dizziness, nausea and low energy are common in the first days or weeks (the keto flu). A study of 300 forum users reported them most often in the first weeks, easing after about 4 weeks; this is not controlled research.
Many ketogenic menus leave out whole food groups, such as fruit, whole grains and pulses. Nutrients, fibre and fluid can fall short without careful planning.
Ketogenic diets in the studies were run with check-ups and blood tests. The studies do not show that a self-started diet gives the same results or safety.
unknowns: No trial has followed people on a ketogenic diet for many years, so the effects on heart attacks, strokes, cancer, bone and kidneys over decades are unknown.
Why LDL cholesterol rises in some people and not others is not understood, and whether it raises heart risk on a keto diet is not known.
Weight and blood sugar benefits faded by 12 months in the diabetes review. It is not clear whether this is because people stop following the diet or the effect wears off.
Claims about a clearer mind, better sport performance, cancer treatment or longer life are not backed by trials in healthy people.
Most studies cannot separate the effect of very low carbohydrate from the effect of eating fewer calories or losing weight.
